en: So with Pi installed and configured, we can
use it.
And here I'm using it without Docker, so not
in a sandbox. You can, as mentioned before,
run it in a sandbox or not, whatever you
want.
Now you can send any prompt you want and you
can ask it to do anything you want on your
machine since it has access to your file
system. It can read files, write files, edit
files. It can do all these things. That's
the idea.
So I could ask it to create an HTML file.
Using vanilla CSS for styling that gives a
quick overview of the core-py features.
And it'll then go ahead and do that. And you
can of course do something else whilst it's
going. You will see what it's doing here. It
is showing some output of course, as you
see.
And you'll see that sometimes there are
additional instructions like pressing Ctrl+O
to expand because it will collapse certain
tool calls. But you can then always follow
those instructions and for example press
Ctrl+O to see step by step which code it is
writing here. And that's not just for
commands or tool calls where it's writing
code. You will see similar instructions in
other situations where you could press
Ctrl+O to expand research results it
gathered or anything like that. So it's
worth carefully analyzing this interface to
get some hints about what you can do.
You can also press Ctrl+P to switch between
different models. Here in the bottom right
corner, you'll see the model. And if I hit
Ctrl+P, it'll switch those models. And
what's worth noting is that this will indeed
switch the model for the currently running
task,
arguably something you'll not do all the
time. But in theory, of course, you could
switch the model if you see it go into a
wrong direction or to have a model that's
better for research tasks initially. And
then once the implementation starts to
switch to a model that's better at
generating the code you want it to generate.
It's also worth noting that Ctrl+P cycles
through. The models that are available for
the provider you registered. Ctrl+L is
another shortcut you can use to get a
dropdown from which you can quickly switch
the model. And if you don't have a running
task, you can of course also use /model for
that.
There also is a /hotkeys command you can run
to quickly see all the hotkeys, all the
shortcuts you can use. Now, I will note
right away that at least in my experience,
depending on which terminal
program you are using, some may not work, or
you may have other processes running on your
system that occupy some of these shortcuts.
But in theory, at least, all these shortcuts
should work and would allow you to easily
navigate when you're typing a longer
message, for example, to jump to the start
of the line of the message you're about to
send, or to quickly change the model, and so
on. So it is, of course, worth taking a look
at these shortcuts to become more acquainted
with Py and work more effectively with it.
With that, it is also done with the task I
gave it here.
So I can open that in my integrated browser
here in Visual Studio Code.
And there I see it generated a nice overview
of some of the core features that make up
Py.
And by the way, I can already tell you that
this extensibility here is one of the most
amazing features by Py, which is why we dive
a lot deeper into that later in the course.
